items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' The closest thing is 'I can kinda book it in and build up your profile and get an idea from there,' which describes what he is doing rather than what the customer should expect. No time estimate, no roadmap, no confirmation ask.

Never asked how she was. She opened with 'Hi, good afternoon. My name is Sunday and I had a question' and volunteered that she is a repeat customer — 'I've used you guys before and you're very wonderful' — which drew a direct move into the trip-fee answer with no acknowledgment of either.

Stairs and floors were never asked at the two pickup addresses. He established the destination is a first-floor apartment, but both Pflugerville origins are private homes and he is collecting a full bedroom set — mattress, box spring, bed frame, two nightstands, a dresser with mirror, and a wardrobe. Whether that bedroom is upstairs at the mother's house is the single biggest variable on a two-and-a-half-hour estimate and it was never asked.

Special considerations never probed — no long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns, no doorway question on a three-piece powered reclining leather sectional, which is exactly the kind of item that does not fit back out the way it came in.
Storage stops never asked.

Access concerns never probed at the destination. It is an apartment complex ('the retreat at Barton creek'), first floor, and he never asked about parking, a loading zone, gate access, or how close a truck can get to unit 2316.
The moving-stressor question was never asked.
The 'pricing is super simple' opener was never used.
The what's-included list was strong but missed gas: 'the trucks, taxes, insurances, the pads, the bands, the wrap to protect everything as well as any tools for any disassemble and reassembly.'

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The job is a leather three-piece powered reclining sectional with electronics inside it and a dresser with an attached mirror — two of the highest-damage-risk item categories there are — and the coverage never came up. The customer even flagged the risk herself when she said the recliners 'will need to be taken apart cause they have electronics in them,' and got 'Not inherently, but not a bad note to put down.'
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite committing to an 8:30 to 9:00 AM start window the customer specifically asked for because of traffic.

The no-hidden-fees pitch was partial. 'No travel charges either which way' and 'there's also no fee if you do need to change the date around' are both real, but the explicit no-credit-card-fee, no-fuel-surcharge, no-assembly-fee list never came.

The clock start was never explained. Lukas covered the minimum and the proration precisely — 'we do have a two and a half hour minimum we charge and then everything else after that gets billed in fifteen minute increments, so you do only pay for the time that gets used' — but never said when billable time begins. On a three-stop job that is the question that matters most: does the clock start at the first Pflugerville address, and does the drive between stops count? The customer never learned either.

No sense-check anywhere, and the cost is visible at the end of the call. After he had already closed twice, the customer circled back genuinely confused: 'they mentioned the Max so $624 but if it's $104 an hour and maybe less, okay. Yeah, the Max is like they charge us like a Max number if they reach over three hours, you said.' She had come away believing $624 was a cap rather than a three-hour scenario. A 'does that make sense?' after the range would have caught it three minutes earlier.

The stated range moved mid-call without explanation. He first said 'two and a half to three hours would be a pretty fair estimate' and priced exactly that ($520 to $624), then later told her 'I said an estimated between the two and a half to three and a half hours is what I think it would take.' Those are different ranges and the second one has no price attached to it — a 3.5-hour day is $728, a number she never heard.
Truck count never stated.
Walk distance never asked at any of the three addresses, and no equivalents or plain-language anchors used.

Traffic was raised by the customer and dropped by the rep. She said 'I feel like the earlier we start maybe the better for traffic' and got 'For sure. Yeah, we have morning and afternoon availability.' The route is Pflugerville to Pflugerville to South Lamar — two crossings of Austin in a morning — and the estimate never moved for it.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent. The carload tip is arguably not applicable here because she is collecting furniture from relatives' homes rather than packing her own household, but the prep half applies fully and was never said: clear the path at both pickups, have the bedroom emptied of loose items and the nightstand drawers emptied before the crew arrives, take the cushions off the sectional, make sure someone with a key is at each address. On a job priced at the two-and-a-half-hour minimum, fifteen minutes of waiting at the mother's house is the difference between the estimate holding and not.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections' — a real miss on a three-address job where he transcribed two street names phonetically ('Sims brook,' 'Manish') and the customer spelled one of them out letter by letter. Those addresses are the job.
Hours of operation never given, though the callback path was otherwise well covered.
Customer's name never used once. Not in the greeting, not in the close. He gave his own name three times.
top_strength: Lukas built this estimate out loud, stop by stop, instead of asserting a range — and it is the most transparent estimate construction in this week's sample. After mapping the route he reasoned through it in front of the customer: 'I think like the first location just to get the couch disassembled and wrapped up might be thirty minutes, drive over to the next place. It might take like an hour to get all that loaded up and padded and protected and loaded up onto the truck. It's a thirty minute drive give or take from Pflugerville down to the apartment, that kind of puts us around that hour and a half, two hour mark. And then about like an hour or so to unload. So I would say two and a half to three hours would be a pretty fair estimate.' A customer who hears the arithmetic can sanity-check it; a customer who hears only 'two and a half to three hours' has to take it on faith. He then priced both ends explicitly — '$520 and if it even goes to three hours the estimated total will be $624' — so she had a floor and a ceiling, not just a number. The second real strength is that he solved a problem the customer did not know she had. She called South Austin about a job that starts in Pflugerville, and rather than quoting the trip fees that would have applied, he worked out the branch routing in her favor and told her so: 'if we run it through our North Austin location, there's no travel charges on anything so we got two plus there, ultimately it all falls within that free service zone.' He had already been transparent about the fees before he found the workaround — 'there would be a travel charge due to the drive in between, I think from South Austin to Pflugerville that's $75... and then there might be a similar $75 travel charge to get down to South Austin as well' — which is what made the eventual zero credible rather than salesy. When she circled back to double-check ('it doesn't matter if we use the South Austin or North Austin location for price?'), he confirmed it flatly: 'Correct, yeah, there's no travel charge either which way.' His address capture is also the best on any call this week — three full addresses with zips, a unit number, a floor, a complex name, and an itemized inventory per stop, read back as a route: 'that's the way I have you built out, to start at the Sims Brook, go to the Manish and then go to South Lamar.' And the moment that most deserves repeating is his handling of the price question at the very end. Rather than defending the higher number to protect himself, he told her the truth about which end of the range he actually believed: 'I said an estimate between two and a half to three and a half hours is what I think it would take on the day. So ultimately, I don't see this job taking over three hours. I think the minimum is quite doable but I don't like to make promises I can't keep. So I would just kind of play a little bit the safe side but I think 520 is very, very doable on the day.' That is a rep talking a customer down toward a lower number because it is the honest one. The customer's verdict on the whole call: 'Oh my gosh, I love you guys. You're the best movers.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: the No Worries Damage Coverage never came up, and this inventory is practically a demonstration case for it. A three-piece powered reclining leather sectional with electronics that has to be disassembled, plus a dresser with an attached mirror, carried out of two houses and into an apartment. She even named the risk herself — 'they're reclining couches so they will need to be taken apart cause they have electronics in them, they're full leather. I don't know if that matters' — and the answer was 'Not inherently, but not a bad note to put down.' The answer that was sitting there: 'It matters to us — powered recliners and mirrored dressers are the two things we're most careful with, and every Einstein move includes No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, already in the rate. Most movers cover you at sixty cents a pound, which on a leather sectional is nothing.' Second priority: ask about stairs at the pickup addresses. He collected a complete bedroom set from a private home and never asked what floor it was on, then priced the whole job at two and a half to three hours. If that bedroom is upstairs this estimate is wrong by an hour before anyone touches a truck. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-four review, and it is the underestimate side of the pattern: Lukas budgeted thirty minutes of drive time each way between Pflugerville and South Lamar. That is not a thirty-minute drive in a loaded box truck on a weekday morning — the customer herself raised traffic ('the earlier we start maybe the better for traffic') and the estimate did not move. Add the unasked stair question, an apartment-complex unload with no parking or access confirmed, and a sectional that has to come apart and go back together, and 'two and a half hours is pretty doable' is optimistic. He then compounded it by telling her at the close that he thinks $520 is 'very, very doable,' which anchors her to the minimum. This is the exact shape of the apartment-underestimate half of the 46 percent problem — short-distance, small-inventory jobs quoted at the floor because nothing about them sounds hard. Worth pulling the actual against this one specifically; if it runs past three hours, it is a clean case study for the bottom-four sessions because the reasoning is all on the tape and easy to walk back through with the rep. The honest-estimating instinct here is right and should be protected — the fix is better inputs, not less candor. Third, tighten the close. Lukas ran three separate 'any other questions' closes and the call still ended with the customer confused about whether $624 was a maximum. One sense-check in the right place — 'so two and a half hours is $520, three hours is $624, and you only pay for what we actually use. Does that make sense?' — replaces all three. Fourth, use her name. She never heard 'Sunday' once across thirteen minutes, and when she said 'Oh my gosh, I love you guys. You're the best movers,' the reply was 'I appreciate that, but alrighty.' A repeat customer handing you a five-star line deserves more than that — 'Sunday, that means a lot. I'll make sure the crew knows you asked for us again' costs nothing and is the reason she calls a third time.
phone_presence_notes: Straightforward, honest and unhurried, with real credibility in the way he refused to overpromise ('I don't like to make promises I can't keep'), but the warmth in this call is coming almost entirely from the customer's side — his language runs clipped and procedural ('Negative,' 'Correct,' 'Alrighty' five separate times), he never used her name once, he let both her repeat-customer compliment at the open and her 'I love you guys, you're the best movers' at the close pass with a flat 'I appreciate that but alrighty,' and he did not acknowledge the traffic worry she raised.
audio_review_reason: There is a real mismatch between what the transcript shows and how the customer reacted. On text alone Lukas reads as procedural and clipped, yet the customer opened by saying she had used Einstein before because 'you're very wonderful' and closed with 'Oh my gosh, I love you guys. You're the best movers' — a 5-level satisfaction signal against 3-level transcript language. Either his delivery carries warmth the words do not, or her enthusiasm is about the brand rather than this rep, and that distinction matters before this score is used in coaching. The end of the call also loops twice over the same $520 versus $624 question with garbled turns ('Oh, what you need? They mentioned the Max so $624'), so it is unclear from text whether the confusion was hers, his, or the transcription's.
